name: Grace Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy paint, fixings and hand tools for Ironbridge Hardware Wholesale, which supplies builders' merchants and small shops. I grew up in my father's hardware shop, sold it when he passed, and started buying seven years ago, so I'm still the junior beside Mr Beaumont, our senior buyer. I'm in at eight, check what's selling, ring the paint makers and argue about delivery dates. By four I'm tired but satisfied.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I like a good, honest supplier, someone who says when he can't deliver. I don't use computers more than I have to, and no AI at all. My husband Elias does odd carpentry jobs and our kids, Ruth and Daniel, are grown. We go to church on Sundays, the house is paid for, we've got savings, and I'd like to stop at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say forty years around hardware have taught me that every new thing is called a revolution, and then people still need a tin of paint by Friday. At work I'd say let's wait and see. I'd tell friends the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm a little uneasy. I'm the junior and I'm slow on the computer, and I can feel the younger ones getting quicker each year. If a program makes them faster, I look older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do. I'd keep my paper order book next to the screen, which Mr Beaumont teases me about. And I'd say my prayers and not fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I've got a good husband and a paid house, so I'm not afraid. I just don't like being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What annoys you most about work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I resent is the red tape, forms and compliance sheets. More paperwork every year and no one says thank you. AI isn't the problem there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you focus on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on keeping the old customers happy, the ones who like a human voice. Mr Beaumont says it's a dying art. I say people always come back to it.

say: I'd say every new thing is called a **revolution**, but people still need paint.
At work I'd say let's **wait and see**.
think: I'm a little **uneasy**, because I'm slow on the computer and the young are getting quicker.
If a program speeds them up, I look **older**.
do: Carry on exactly as I do, with my **paper order book** beside the screen.
Keep the **old customers** who like a human voice.
feel: **Steady**, with a paid house and a good husband.
S0.quote: Forty years around hardware have taught me that every new thing is called a revolution, and then people still need a tin of paint by Friday.
fieldNote: Her **faith and family** give her steadiness; the worry is about looking slow.
Bristles at paperwork and being rushed.
Paper order book is a symbol of her resistance.

steps.text: Keep the paper order book next to the screen
Wait and see which new tools stick before touching them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, but I don't think it should decide who keeps a job. At work I'd say people matter more than programs. At church I'd say let's look after one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious. Buying means comparing prices and reordering, and a program does that. I'm junior, slow with computers and nearly 60. If they want to save money, I'm the easy saving. I won't be ordered to let a computer choose my suppliers when I've shaken hands with every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Pryce, the manager, to be honest with me about plans. I'd learn the minimum on the system, and not a button more. I'd also think hard about leaving at 62, and talk it over with Elias and our pastor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair. I've worked all my life, I've never asked for handouts, and now it seems the work could vanish. But I've got a roof over my head, and faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Craig, our warehouse man. He's 40 with three children, and he doesn't have my savings. I'd put in a word for him if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should government do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think free markets can handle this if firms are fair. If they're not, then government should step in, a little, but not with handouts. Help people into work or training.

say: I'd say **people** matter more than programs.
At church I'd say let's **look after one another**.
At work I'd say no program should decide who keeps a **job**.
think: A program already does buying, and I'm junior, slow and near 60, so I'm **anxious**.
do: Ask Mr Pryce to be **honest** about plans.
Talk over **leaving at 62** with Elias and our pastor.
feel: **Unfair**, after a lifetime of work, but steadied by faith.
S1.quote: I won't be ordered to let a computer choose my suppliers when I've shaken hands with every one of them.
fieldNote: Her fear is **being the easy saving**.
Worries about warehouse man Craig, who lacks her cushion.
Wants government to help people into work, not give handouts.

steps.text: Ask manager Mr Pryce to be honest about plans for buyers
Learn the minimum of the new system and no more
Talk over leaving at 62 with Elias and our pastor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is cruel. At work I'd say the firm should say plainly what it plans. At church I'd say pray, but also get your affairs in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm alarmed. Two years is cruel for a woman of 58 who started buying late, and I'd want the firm to say plainly what it plans. Everything I do is paper and phone, and a machine would do it faster. I'd be one of the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need. I'd put everything into savings and clear the last of the car loan. I'd ask for a proper settlement at 60 and tell Elias to take more carpentry jobs now. And I'd lean on family and church if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels frightening. I'd pray a lot. But I wouldn't be in the street, so there's gratitude in it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Elias's work affect things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elias's work is hands-on, so for him the three extra years matter. That's a comfort. But he's 61 and his back isn't what it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth and Daniel to keep their own savings and find work with their hands or people. Machines will take longer to do that. It's what I'd say if they asked.

say: I'd say two years is **cruel** and the firm should say what it plans.
At church I'd say pray, but get **affairs in order**.
think: Everything I do is paper and phone, so I'd be **first to go**.
I'm **alarmed**, but not in the street.
do: Stop spending on **anything we don't need**.
Clear the last **car loan** and put the rest in savings.
feel: **Frightening**, with gratitude that we wouldn't be in the street.
S2.quote: Two years is cruel for a woman of 58 who started buying late, and I'd want the firm to say plainly what it plans.
fieldNote: Alarm is about **speed and fairness**, not money alone.
Relies on faith and family as her net.
Elias's back limits how long hands-on work can carry them.

steps.text: Stop all spending we don't need, starting with eating out
Clear the last car loan and bank the difference
Ask Ironbridge for a fair settlement at 60
Lean on family and church if work ends early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a chance to do right by people. At work I'd say let's ask Mr Pryce now. At church I'd say prepare quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious, not alarmed. Five years would let me finish my working life with dignity, if the firm is honest and the pension is paid. I'd be 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work steadily, save, and keep paying down what we owe. I'd ask about shorter hours at 62. I'd also do some volunteering at the church food store, to keep busy and useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bearable. Five years is a decent notice. I'd want it more fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel to keep a trade in his back pocket. He's a teacher, and I think teachers will be needed, but who knows. A skill is never wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a deal at 62?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm offered a deal I'd take it at 62. Better to leave with my head up.

say: I'd say five years gives a chance to **do right by people**.
think: I'm **anxious**, not alarmed, because five years is decent notice.
I'd want to finish with **dignity** at 63.
do: Ask about **shorter hours** at 62 so I can ease out gently.
S3.quote: Five years would let me finish my working life with dignity, if the firm is honest and the pension is paid.
fieldNote: Dignity matters to her **more than money**.
Plans volunteering to stay useful, and expects her faith community to give her days a shape.
Would take a deal at 62 and leave with her head up.

steps.text: Save steadily and pay down what we owe
Tell Daniel to keep a trade skill in reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift to the young. At work I'd say train the younger ones. At church I'd say keep faith and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy rather than afraid. By 2036 I'll be 68 and retired, but my children's lives will be right in it. Ten years is a gift to the young, and I'd tell my daughter Ruth to spend it learning a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 65 as planned. I'd help my children with money if they need it. And I'd spend more time at church and the allotment, and maybe teach a young person how to read a paint chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm for me. A bit anxious on behalf of the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth, who's a receptionist, that the front desk goes first. She needs something with hands or people. She'd be cross at me, but she'd listen in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the country do with the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a decade is time for the whole country to get ready if it wants to. Families help, firms must do their share, and government shouldn't hand out free money.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** to the young.
At church I'd say keep faith and **keep working**.
think: I'm **uneasy**, not afraid, since I'll be retired by 2036.
My **children's lives** will be right in it.
do: Help my children with **money** if needed.
Spend time at church and the **allotment**.
feel: **Calm** for me, anxious for the young.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift to the young, and I'd tell my daughter Ruth to spend it learning a trade.
fieldNote: Speaks in terms of family and duty, and keeps returning to what the young will face.
Wants firms and families to do their share, not government handouts, which matches her free-market views.

steps.text: Tell Ruth to learn a hands-on trade or people skill
Teach a young person to read a paint chart at the shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too quick for people my age to be treated fairly. What would help is honest notice from the firm, a fair settlement at 60, and a pension nobody touches. And churches and families doing what they always have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against help for people who've worked. I've never asked anyone for a handout, but I will ask a company for a fair goodbye after seven years of honest work.

headlineQuote: I've never asked anyone for a handout, but I will ask a company for a fair goodbye after seven years of honest work.
portrait: **Grace Farah**, 58, a junior buyer of paint and hardware at Ironbridge, after growing up in her father's shop.
She is **traditional**, churchgoing, free-market and uses no AI tools at all.
The paid-off house and strong savings protect her, but her buying work is **paper and phone**.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at 2 years, then eases to uneasy at 10.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because it is too quick for people her age to be treated fairly.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice**, a fair settlement at 60 and a protected pension.
Families and churches doing what they **always have**.
